article_title: Collaborative Learning: An Alternative Approach to Adult Literacy Instruction.
citation: Philadelphia Mayor's Commission on Literacy. (1994). Collaborative Learning: An Alternative Approach to Adult Literacy Instruction. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED376329
title: Base initial assessment in real-life contexts using informal, authentic measures alongside standardized testing
description: The guide holds that assessment in collaborative learning should reflect its learner-centered, participatory philosophy. "Assessment is situated in real-life contexts and relevant to what learners already know in their everyday lives," and informal assessment is supportive and focuses on each learner's strengths. Practitioners use authentic reading selections and writing tasks (newspapers, shopping lists, notes) to gauge abilities, and "informal, alternative, and authentic assessment is primarily used in addition to standardized testing."
requirements: Intake interviews, intake forms, authentic reading and writing tasks, and goals and self-assessment formats completed with learners
constraints: Standardized testing may still be required, in which case informal assessment is used in conjunction with it
target_learners: Adult basic education learners entering literacy programs
target_learning_goals: Identifying learner strengths, goals, and instructional needs
examples: The guide adapts its intake and assessment material from Auerbach (1990) and Lyte, et. al. (1986) and provides intake, goal-setting, and action-plan forms in its appendix
key_sources: Philadelphia Mayor's Commission on Literacy. (1994). Collaborative Learning: An Alternative Approach to Adult Literacy Instruction. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED376329

article_title: PowerSchool Attendance Intervention (Family Engagement)
citation: PowerSchool Attendance Intervention. (2024). PowerSchool Attendance Intervention program description and evidence summary. https://www.powerschool.com/
title: Teacher-mediated automated attendance messaging pattern combining dashboards, templates, and two-way family communication
description: The intervention operationalizes attendance improvement as a teacher-family communication workflow: educators monitor daily and period-level attendance and chronic absenteeism data, then use customized messaging templates with automatically populated parent or student names and real-time attendance data, delivered via two-way texting and email. Auto-translation features help administrators and treatment teachers reach parents from diverse backgrounds. This pattern reduces the time burden for school staff while keeping communication personalized and data-driven.
requirements: Access to a school or district administrative system to gather attendance data
Teachers and administrators trained via the Train-the-Trainer methodology
constraints: Effectiveness evidence comes from a semester-long RCT in 3 DC public schools with 6th-12th grade students; in-seat attendance effects were insignificant.
target_learners: 6th-12th grade students and their families
examples: Teachers in the treatment condition used the app and training to communicate with families, while control teachers communicated with parents as usual.
key_sources: PowerSchool Attendance Intervention. (2024). PowerSchool Attendance Intervention program description and evidence summary. https://www.powerschool.com/

article_title: PowerSchool Attendance Intervention
citation: PowerSchool Attendance Intervention. (2024). Evidence for ESI program review. https://www.evidenceforessi.org/
title: Automate personalization of family communication templates to reduce staff time burden
description: The review states that "[t]he ability to automatically populate a parent or student's name and real-time attendance data into communication templates greatly reduces the time burden for school staff." Attendance-communication tools should therefore pull names and live attendance data into message templates automatically, so educators can send accurate, personalized family messages at scale without manual entry.
requirements: Access to a school or district administrative system supplying real-time attendance data and family contact information.
target_learners: 6th-12th grade students and their families
target_learning_goals: Increasing family engagement and supporting student attendance
examples: The PowerSchool Attendance Intervention app auto-populates parent or student names and real-time attendance data into messaging templates used for two-way text and email communication with families.

article_title: Authentic Intellectual Work and Standardized Tests
citation: Fred M. Newmann, Anthony S. Bryk, Jenny K. Nagaoka. (2001). Authentic Intellectual Work and Standardized Tests: Conflict or Coexistence? Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://www.consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Organize instruction around authentic intellectual work rather than choosing between basic skills and ambitious intellectual work
description: The report argues that the debate posing basic-skills teaching against ambitious intellectual work "rests on a false dichotomy." Its evidence shows that "organizing instruction around challenging, authentic intellectual work can achieve both goals simultaneously": students produced more complex work and also achieved greater gains on standardized tests of basic skills. The principle directs teachers, administrators, and policymakers to emphasize authentic assignments without fearing basic-skills losses.
requirements: Assignments must meet the three AIW criteria: construction of knowledge, disciplined inquiry, and value beyond school
constraints: Evidence comes from writing and mathematics in grades 3, 6, and 8 of disadvantaged Chicago elementary schools; high-quality assignments were not commonplace in the Chicago Public Schools
target_learners: elementary students in grades 3, 6, and 8 in disadvantaged urban schools
target_learning_goals: basic skills in reading and mathematics alongside complex intellectual work
examples: The study linked scored writing and mathematics assignments from 19 Chicago elementary schools to ITBS and IGAP outcomes for almost 5,000 students, finding higher gains in high-quality-assignment classrooms
key_sources: Fred M. Newmann, Anthony S. Bryk, Jenny K. Nagaoka. (2001). Authentic Intellectual Work and Standardized Tests: Conflict or Coexistence? Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/authentic-intellectual-work-and-standardized-tests-conflict-or-coexistence

article_title: Achieving School Reform in Chicago
citation: Consortium on Chicago School Research. (1991). Achieving School Reform in Chicago: What We Need To Know — A Research Agenda. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Assessment should move beyond standardized tests toward authentic measures such as portfolios and projects
description: Stakeholders in the consultation process expressed dissatisfaction with the ITBS as too narrow and voiced widespread interest in new measures of student performance that move beyond paper-and-pencil standardized tests. The report recommends investigating authentic measures such as portfolios and projects, linked to clearly articulated objectives, warning that without such progress Chicago will be left with a minimalist accounting system. The Consortium recommends immediate and sustained attention to revamping testing and assessment.
requirements: Assessment must be linked to a clearly articulated set of objectives establishing what an individual should know and be able to do
constraints: Testing is mired in controversies about purpose, validity and reliability of measurement, test security, cost, and information use and abuse, which must be confronted for adequate measures of learning
target_learners: Chicago Public Schools students in grades one through twelve
target_learning_goals: measuring higher order thinking skills, problem solving, and communication alongside basic skills
examples: The Chicago Teachers' Union advocated abandoning standardized testing for primary grades and encouraging instructionally focused processes such as portfolios and instruments allowing creative thinking and expression
key_sources: Consortium on Chicago School Research. (1991). Achieving School Reform in Chicago: What We Need To Know — A Research Agenda. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/achieving-school-reform-chicago-what-we-need-know

article_title: Empowering High School Communities to Evaluate Their Programs Through Alumni Surveys
citation: Shelton Daal, Emi Iwatani, Tiffany Leones. (2024). Empowering High School Communities to Evaluate Their Programs Through Alumni Surveys. Digital Promise. https://bit.ly/AlumRefs
title: Authentic co-design is not rushed or forced, and there is untapped knowledge everywhere in school communities.
description: The brief's main takeaways state that "Authentic Co-Design is not Rushed or Forced" and that "There is Untapped Knowledge Everywhere". This principle holds that co-design processes must move at the community's pace rather than a researcher-imposed timeline, and that community members across roles — students, alumni, teachers, administrators, parents, community partners — hold valuable knowledge for designing evaluations of their own programs.
requirements: Allow community members to drive the process at their own pace
Engage a wide range of community stakeholders as design partners
target_learners: high school community members, including youth and adults, participating in research-practice partnerships
target_learning_goals: designing program evaluations, such as alumni surveys, that reflect community knowledge
examples: The brief lists these two statements as its Main Takeaways, alongside future work on using survey results for healing through strength identification, program improvement, and making use of existing networks.
key_sources: Shelton Daal, Emi Iwatani, Tiffany Leones. (2024). Empowering High School Communities to Evaluate Their Programs Through Alumni Surveys. Digital Promise. https://bit.ly/AlumRefs

article_title: Designing for Technology Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Take a problem-solving orientation with authentic practice, immediate application, and feedback
description: Because adult learning is rooted in experience, the report recommends structuring problems on what learners encounter in work and life, then helping them practice strategies to solve them: "the more learners can practice in authentic situations and apply what they learn immediately, the more likely they are to develop new skills."
requirements: Build assessments and feedback loops into the problem-solving environment; the report states this "helps students monitor their learning."
constraints: Learners must be free to make mistakes while solving problems; the report ties making mistakes, reflecting, and trying another approach to building persistence.
target_learners: adult learners preparing for work in fields such as healthcare
low-skilled adult learners
target_learning_goals: problem-solving strategies for work and life situations
examples: A Pine Technical College game trains medical-career students through realistic avatar scenarios — dealing with death and sickness, talking to patients, engaging family members — with feedback on each choice and retries until the desired behavior occurs.
key_sources: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/bb3f892f-a74d-4da1-8086-0334fd227316

article_title: The Impact of the Mindsets Mathematics Program on Student Engagement, Ability to Reason, and Repeated Reasoning
citation: Gage, N. (2025). The impact of the Mindsets mathematics program on student engagement, ability to reason, and repeated reasoning. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Embed mathematics reasoning in authentic, real-world collaborative tasks with mixed-grade groupings to support engagement and equitable access
description: The report argues that mathematics learning environments should use context-rich, problem-based tasks rather than deficit-oriented remediation. The Mindsets design situates challenges in real-world contexts, uses mixed-grade groupings so older students revisit foundational content while supporting younger students, and is "intended to allow students to engage meaningfully and reduce the stigma often associated with remediation." The authors state this supports equitable mathematics instruction that rejects remediation models.
requirements: Access to meaningful tasks, high expectations, and supportive teacher facilitation
constraints: Evidence comes from a single 5-week summer implementation in one district; the authors call for broader consideration and replication
target_learners: middle school students in grades 6–8, including students needing prior-year skill development
examples: Most sessions were conducted in mixed-grade groupings, allowing older students to revisit foundational content while supporting younger students' preparation for middle school rigor
key_sources: Gage, N. (2025). The impact of the Mindsets mathematics program on student engagement, ability to reason, and repeated reasoning. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED677579

article_title: Task Automation, Worker Augmentation: Opportunities for Career and Technical Education in the Heartland
citation: Jacobs, B. (2026, September). Task automation, worker augmentation: Opportunities for career and technical education in the heartland. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/317
title: Augmentation, automation, and displacement are distinct outcomes that CTE planning must not conflate
description: The brief defines three distinct concepts often used interchangeably: automation is the underlying technical capability of whether AI can perform a task, while augmentation and displacement describe human employment outcomes. Augmentation is "a scenario in which AI absorbs specific tasks within a job while the worker keeps the role," whereas displacement eliminates the position itself. The brief argues mistaking one for the other leads CTE programs to either abandon strong occupational tracks prematurely or credential students for disappearing roles.
requirements: CTE programs, employers, and policymakers must apply the distinction when making multi-year curriculum and investment decisions
constraints: The distinction concerns employment outcomes once AI capability is put to use, not the capability itself
target_learners: CTE students in Heartland-region secondary and postsecondary programs
target_learning_goals: Preparing learners for future-forward, automation-resilient employment in a labor market defined by change
examples: The brief treats occupations shaped by augmentation as future-ready, automation-resilient employment: work built to flex with the technology rather than compete against it
key_sources: Jacobs, B. (2026, September). Task automation, worker augmentation: Opportunities for career and technical education in the heartland. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/317

article_title: Design Principles for Instructionally Relevant Assessment Systems
citation: Badrinarayan, A. (2024). Design principles for instructionally relevant assessment systems. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/111.528
title: Authentic assessment tasks centering disciplinary sensemaking
description: The Authentic principle holds that assessments should "highlight and center the key concepts, modes of inquiry, and ways of learning in the discipline." Systems that center authenticity use tasks representing authentic disciplinary activities, assess sensible bundles of standards contributing to substantive performance, and prioritize depth over breadth, rather than relying on selected-response proxies for performance or superficial contrived contexts. Critical features include high-quality performance tasks, emphasizing sensemaking over covering the breadth of standards, and focusing on the most-needed instructional shifts for the grade band.
requirements: High-quality performance tasks as a component of state assessment systems
constraints: State assessments are described as a relatively blunt instrument to guide change; efforts to do it all have resulted in assessments unsuccessful at compelling instructional change
target_learners: K-12 students, with examples drawn from science assessment
target_learning_goals: Engagement with science and engineering practices and crosscutting concepts
examples: Science assessments foregrounding science and engineering practices, emphasizing using scientific ideas to make sense of data and distinguish validity of claims
key_sources: Badrinarayan, A. (2024). Design principles for instructionally relevant assessment systems. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/111.528

article_title: 5 Things for Advocates to Know about Chronic Absenteeism
citation: EdTrust. (2023). 5 Things for Advocates to Know About Chronic Absenteeism. https://EdTrust.org
title: Reducing chronic absence requires authentic partnerships with students, families, and communities
description: This principle holds that schools cannot solve attendance problems alone. The brief states "Unless school leaders draw upon the knowledge of their students and families, they are unlikely to create effective solutions, especially given the diverse and rapidly changing realities that affect student attendance." Schools should partner with community organizations and public agencies to resolve barriers to attendance and build relationships, engaging marginalized communities in co-developing solutions.
requirements: Strong relationships with students and families, especially from marginalized communities
Educators and staff examining their own biases and learning about students' and families' identities and experiences
constraints: Effective only when engagement is authentic co-development rather than top-down; the brief stresses drawing on family knowledge
target_learners: Students from marginalized communities
K-12 students facing attendance barriers
examples: The brief recommends organizing youth and families to work with schools and districts to identify attendance barriers and develop solutions, and asking for state funding and technical assistance to forge authentic partnerships.
key_sources: EdTrust. (2023). 5 Things for Advocates to Know About Chronic Absenteeism. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED627994

article_title: AI in the Wild: A Large Scale Analysis of Authentic Interactions of College Students with Generative AI
citation: Taelin Karidi, Ofra Amir, and Ido Roll. (2026). AI in the Wild: A Large Scale Analysis of Authentic Interactions of College Students with Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.29442
title: Large-scale dataset of authentic student–AI chat logs from six Technion courses
description: The article analyzes a dataset of authentic student–AI interactions collected from undergraduate courses at the Technion – Israel Institute of Technology, comprising "821 students, 2,078 submitted chat logs, and 15,887 interaction turns across multiple domains". Students voluntarily submitted chat logs generated while working on course assignments, without instructions on how to use AI tools; participation was incentivized with minor course credit (up to 2%) with an alternative assignment for non-users. All materials are available at https://osf.io/z9hqb/.
requirements: Students voluntarily submitted chat logs; submissions were independent of course staff and anonymized, with IRB approval.
constraints: Participation was voluntary, raising possible selection effects; the study covers a limited number of courses.
target_learners: undergraduate students across multiple academic domains
target_learning_goals: understanding how generative AI is integrated into students' learning practices
examples: Course-level logs range from 124 turns (English) to 4,106 turns (Probability), with turns per log from 6.2±6.1 to 26.8±24.2.
key_sources: Taelin Karidi, Ofra Amir, and Ido Roll. (2026). AI in the Wild: A Large Scale Analysis of Authentic Interactions of College Students with Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.29442

article_title: Toward Accessible Psychotherapy Training Using AI-Driven Interactive Patient Avatars
citation: Pascal Riachi, Sofie Kamber, Stella Brogna, Andrew Gloster, Rafael Wampfler. (2026). Toward Accessible Psychotherapy Training Using AI-Driven Interactive Patient Avatars. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17786
title: Automated turn-by-turn ACT fidelity feedback mechanism with balance indicator and retry option
description: GPT-4o mini evaluates each therapist utterance from the third turn onward, scoring all 25 ACT-FM items on a 0–3 scale across four paired dimensions and aggregating them into an ACT balance score (ACT-consistent minus ACT-inconsistent totals). Feedback appears as a visual balance indicator; when balance is negative, a modal dialog pauses the session with a rationale and offers retry or continue, and selecting retry removes the most recent utterance so the therapist can reformulate.
requirements: Sufficient conversational context, which is why feedback starts from the third therapist turn
Structured prompt framing the model as an ACT clinical supervisor
constraints: Feedback was occasionally too narrow when therapist utterances reflected preparatory steps rather than complete interventions
target_learners: Psychotherapists in training
Practicing psychotherapists
target_learning_goals: Awareness of therapeutic language and intervention choices
examples: The retry option removes the most recent utterance, allowing reformulation and immediate observation of alternative interventions' effects on the ACT score.
key_sources: Pascal Riachi, Sofie Kamber, Stella Brogna, Andrew Gloster, Rafael Wampfler. (2026). Toward Accessible Psychotherapy Training Using AI-Driven Interactive Patient Avatars. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17786

article_title: AI Literacy for Legal Translation: Developing Digital Resilience
citation: Łucja Biel. (2026). AI Literacy for Legal Translation: Developing Digital Resilience. University of Warsaw. https://uw.edu.pl
title: Use AI in legal translation as augmentation that preserves human control, not unsupervised automation
description: The chapter argues that legal accountability requires human-centred augmentation rather than unsupervised automation. As printed: "Augmentation refers to the use of AI to support professional judgement while preserving human control over translation decisions". Because legal translation carries professional responsibility and legal accountability, and errors may have severe consequences, automation that replaces human decision-making cannot satisfy these requirements. The principle underpins the AI literacy framework, whose strategic dimension governs whether, when and how AI should be used.
requirements: Translators retain responsibility for the final translation and exercise informed professional judgement over AI output
constraints: The chapter notes attitudes of authorities towards AI use remain inconsistent, and courts have held machine-translated evidence deficient where knowing, voluntary consent could not be guaranteed
target_learners: legal translators
legal translation students
examples: The chapter cites US case law (United States v. Cruz-Zamora; United States v. Ramirez-Mendoza) where Google Translate-mediated police interactions were held deficient
key_sources: Łucja Biel. (2026). AI Literacy for Legal Translation: Developing Digital Resilience. University of Warsaw. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04641

article_title: ASE-26: A Curriculum for Agentic Software Engineering as a Discipline
citation: Mikael Gorsky (Holon Institute of Technology). (2026). ASE-26: a curriculum for agentic software engineering as a discipline.
title: Auditability principle and the seven-part anatomy of an agentic workflow turn
description: The article defines auditability as the discipline's defining principle: "a workflow that cannot be inspected, replayed or evaluated after the fact is craft, while engineering is accountable and reproducible." Its operational artefact is the audit trail, a frozen record linking intent to specification, context, agent trajectory and verification, which agentic work produces as a byproduct of normal operation. Each workflow turn has seven constituents running as a single act rather than sequential phases: intent, specification, context, plan, execution, verification and the audit trail, each with a corresponding curriculum module.
requirements: The practitioner must preserve, name and make navigable the material the workflow generates, so someone other than the original engineer can reconstruct what was decided, why, and what happened
constraints: The article notes classical software engineering struggled to produce audit trails routinely because engineers wrote them by hand after the fact; the principle's low cost depends on agent-generated records
target_learners: undergraduate software engineering students
examples: Module 4 names the seven-part anatomy and the auditability principle; Module 13 develops verification gates with verification theatre as a named failure mode
key_sources: Mikael Gorsky (Holon Institute of Technology). (2026). ASE-26: a curriculum for agentic software engineering as a discipline. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01152

article_title: The Effect of High-Frequency, Automatically-marked Formative Assessments on Student Outcomes in A-Level Sciences
citation: Matey Yordanov, Mikhail Bychkov, and Andrei Kuchma. (2026). The Effect of High-Frequency, Automatically-marked Formative Assessments on Student Outcomes in A-Level Sciences. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23566
title: Deploy automated marking as a high-speed formative loop accelerator to decouple assessment frequency from human grading capacity
description: The article proposes that fully automated marking of complex handwritten STEM work functions as "a high-speed ''formative loop accelerator''": it does not replace the educator but collapses feedback latency from nearly two weeks to under 2 hours and enables a fourfold increase in retrieval practice volume. This decouples assessment frequency from staffing constraints, letting institutions run rigorous mock examination programmes without inflating staff workloads or precipitating teacher burnout.
requirements: An automated grading platform capable of parsing unstructured handwritten STEM notation and applying official mark schemes
Students must handwrite responses on paper to preserve cognitive fidelity of examination conditions
constraints: The study could not isolate the discrete impact of automated feedback quality from the increase in practice volume
Whether high-frequency human feedback would yield identical results remains unknown
target_learners: Upper-secondary A-Level STEM students in international secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Improved final mock examination outcomes and exam readiness in STEM A-Level subjects
examples: The intervention cohort completed weekly or bi-weekly practice exercises and partial mock examinations marked automatically over a 16-week term, while the control cohort completed two human-graded mocks
key_sources: Matey Yordanov, Mikhail Bychkov, and Andrei Kuchma. (2026). The Effect of High-Frequency, Automatically-marked Formative Assessments on Student Outcomes in A-Level Sciences. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23566

article_title: Argus: Academic Integrity in the Era of Generative AI
citation: David Racovan, Ajay Rawat, Christopher K. May, Jeffrey A. Turkstra. (2026). Argus: Academic Integrity in the Era of Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36073
title: Pair any automated LLM-detection system with a structured human review process before academic integrity action
description: The article argues that automated detection scores should triage rather than decide cases: "We argue that any automated detection system must be accompanied by a structured process for human review." Because a false accusation carries lasting consequences while a missed case affects only one student's learning, the appropriate standard is whether a tool makes human review fast and structured enough to be feasible in large-enrollment courses. Argus operationalizes this by ranking students by H-score, surfacing individual indicators in code context, and requiring manual review by policy before any integrity action.
requirements: Course staff must review flagged cases manually before any academic integrity action; the tool's purpose is to expedite triage, especially where individual review of every student is infeasible.
constraints: The authors accept a non-zero false negative rate; benign behaviors such as prior programming experience or pasting code drafted in an external editor can produce elevated scores.
target_learners: undergraduate students in large-enrollment programming courses
target_learning_goals: efficient triage of suspected LLM-assisted work
examples: In Spring 2026, staff reviewed the top 300 students by H-score plus top-150 per-assignment students, with three reviewers evaluating independently then reaching consensus, and extreme benefit of the doubt given to avoid false positives.
key_sources: David Racovan, Ajay Rawat, Christopher K. May, Jeffrey A. Turkstra. (2026). Argus: Academic Integrity in the Era of Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36073

article_title: Designing for What Cannot Be Seen: Supporting Embodied String Learning for Musicians with Blindness and Low-Vision
citation: Shi Shi, Lingyun Chen, Zitao Zhang, Amanda R. Draper, and Eli Blevis. 2026. Designing for What Cannot Be Seen: Supporting Embodied String Learning for Musicians with Blindness and Low-Vision. The 28th International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18598
title: Augmented bow track with graded friction feedback
description: A speculative clip-on augmentation positioned between the bridge and fingerboard, using two moving tensioners that hold the bow and shift position according to the string being played. Rather than enforcing a fixed path, it makes bow deviation perceptible through graded friction that increases as the bow drifts, aiming to build muscle memory through repeated practice. Envisioned functions include non-visual feedback for drift and contact-point change, continuous low-attention feedback enabling mid-stroke correction, adaptive bow-lane awareness for dynamics, and practice scaffolding with post-practice summaries.
requirements: Must preserve freedom of movement and function as a learning companion rather than define a single correct technique or replace instruction.
constraints: Speculative concept not yet evaluated in deployed contexts; the authors state whether it works in practice remains to be evaluated.
target_learners: Violin and viola learners with blindness and low-vision
target_learning_goals: Straight bow path, contact-point awareness, and bow-lane control for dynamics
examples: Inspired by M1's low-tech rubber band and pencil aid, whose feedback I1 called effective but binary and dependent on teacher supervision.

article_title: Designing for What Cannot Be Seen: Supporting Embodied String Learning for Musicians with Blindness and Low-Vision
citation: Shi Shi, Lingyun Chen, Zitao Zhang, Amanda R. Draper, and Eli Blevis. 2026. Designing for What Cannot Be Seen: Supporting Embodied String Learning for Musicians with Blindness and Low-Vision. The 28th International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18598
title: Augmented bow hold aid with finger pressure force mapping
description: A bow-mounted augmentation preserving the geometry of a traditional frog, using thin-film pressure sensors (e.g., Velostat) to produce a spatial force map across finger contact points and an IMU to capture bow orientation and kinematics. By mapping where pressure concentrates and shifts, the system could infer finger placement and over-gripping patterns and provide real-time, low-attention feedback indicating which contact region is too tense and which finger to relax or reposition. It is framed as a temporary, practice-oriented scaffold for habit-building rather than a permanent replacement for conventional bow hold training.
requirements: Must preserve compatibility with existing bows and minimal disruption to established motor habits, per the article's design rationale.
constraints: The enlarged grip volume is a stated tradeoff: prolonged use may lead players to adapt to a larger grip and feel discomfort returning to an unaugmented bow; M2 cautioned the aid might not transfer when removed and could deform correct posture.
target_learners: Violin and viola learners with blindness and low-vision
target_learning_goals: Relaxed bow hold, balanced load distribution across fingers, and reduced over-gripping
examples: M2 rated the concept positively but warned that hand posture with and without the pinky holder is not the same, drawing on prior experience with rubber attachments altering tactile perception.

citation: Organisciak, P., & Acar, S. (2026). Know when to trust: Making AI scoring more reliable for educational assessment. Behavior Research. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-026-03058-1
title: Alternative Uses Test response dataset of over 20,000 responses from more than 2,000 participants

target_learning_goals: measurement of divergent thinking originality via automated scoring

article_title: Challenges for Musical Education in the Age of AI and Digital Transformation
citation: Jean-Pierre Briot. (2026). Challenges for Musical Education in the Age of AI and Digital Transformation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05176
title: Two approaches to AI in music: autonomous generators versus interactive composition assistants, with distinct educational significance
description: The article distinguishes two philosophies of AI in music. Autonomous generators such as Suno and Udio produce complete pieces from a text prompt, while composition assistants such as FlowComposer and the Continuator support the human creator interactively. The article argues the distinction matters enormously for education: the former positions students as consumers of AI output, while the latter positions AI as an extension of the student's own creative agency. It also notes a fundamental audio-versus-symbolic divide, with symbolic representations being interpretable, controllable, and educationally meaningful.
requirements: Systems in the assistant lineage must allow the composer to retain full intentionality and control over the compositional refinement process
constraints: Autonomous generators are described as end-to-end, requiring complete regeneration for any structural modification, with no lever for intervention at the compositional level
target_learners: music students in higher education and conservatory settings
target_learning_goals: critical evaluation of AI music systems
examples: FlowComposer was validated in the creation of the album Hello World in 2018, subordinated throughout to the artistic vision of professional musicians; the Continuator learned a player's style and continued in that style at performance time

article_title: Scaffolding Systematic Reviews in Learning Design and Technology Through Mentoring and AI Integration
citation: Xiyu Wang, Fatemeh Dadashipour, Basori, Yukiko Maeda, & Jennifer C. Richardson. (2026). Scaffolding systematic reviews in learning design and technology through mentoring and AI integration. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10629-8
title: Treat automation in systematic reviews as a complement rather than a substitute, with careful documentation and human oversight
description: The article concludes that "the automation is best treated as a complement rather than a substitute" in systematic reviews. While automation reduced procedural burdens such as screening, "interpretive decisions still required substantial human oversight." The team tested LLM-based extraction tools (MetaMate) but chose not to integrate them because "currently available tools cannot ensure that the extracted content is verifiably grounded in the original text." Selective use can enhance efficiency while human verification safeguards interpretive rigor and credibility.
requirements: Careful documentation and human oversight to preserve interpretive rigor and credibility; researchers need both technical skills and methodological understanding to leverage emerging tools
constraints: Automation development and effectiveness are uneven across review stages; tasks requiring contextual interpretation, reconciliation of ambiguous reporting, or integrative synthesis remain difficult to automate
target_learners: SR teams in interdisciplinary fields such as LDT
target_learning_goals: balancing efficiency and credibility in technology-supported systematic reviews
examples: The team used Covidence's ML-based prioritization to reorder studies by previous screening decisions, but declined to substitute machine extraction for human coding

citation: Ivo Bueno, Babette Bühler, Philipp Stark, Tim Fütterer, Ulrich Trautwein, Dorottya Demszky, Heather Hill, Enkelejda Kasneci. (2026). From Scoring to Explanations: Evaluating SHAP and LLM Rationales for Rubric-based Teaching Quality Assessment. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05180
title: Position automated rubric-based scoring systems as decision-support tools that augment rather than replace human raters in high-stakes settings
description: The article argues that in high-stakes educational contexts, automated scoring systems "should not replace human raters in high-stakes settings", because models trained on human annotations may inherit subjective judgments or structural biases and propagate them at scale. Instead, such systems "should be positioned as self-assessment or decision-support tools that augment, rather than replace, professional judgment". The article further stresses that scores and explanations are probabilistic and imperfect, and that interpretability methods are intended to support teacher reflection and informed decision-making rather than serve as authoritative assessments.
requirements: Educators and stakeholders must be able to understand how and why a model arrives at a given score, requiring transparency of scores and explanations
constraints: Unchecked deployment in high-stakes settings may create self-reinforcing feedback loops of biased predictions
Model predictions and explanations risk being interpreted as objective ground truth
target_learners: teachers receiving automated feedback on classroom transcripts
target_learning_goals: supporting teacher reflection and informed decision-making about automated teaching quality assessments
examples: The article's ethical considerations section recommends communicating that both scores and explanations are probabilistic and imperfect, and avoiding presenting unvalidated LLM rationales as authoritative interpretations of teaching practice

citation: Du P, Zhou Y, Zhou Z, Wang H and Cao Q (2026). The synthetic position: generative artificial intelligence and the suspension of self-authorship in emerging adulthood. Front. Psychol. 17:1922087. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1922087
title: Authorial suspension: a self densely voiced yet un-authored
description: Authorial suspension is the article's name for the outcome condition: a self whose many voices are articulated and in incessant conversation, but whose integrative act is performed elsewhere, so the person lacks "the felt sense of being the author of the conversation". Suspension carries two senses: held aloft, and deferred, left open. It is identified behaviorally by three markers: a fluency-ownership gap, deferral of commitment despite exhausted deliberation, and an overview unavailable when the system is withdrawn.
requirements: Identification requires behavioral markers: the withdrawal probe, in which a person must convene the inner conversation without the system, is reserved for the third marker
constraints: It is a disturbance in the locus of authorship, not in its presence, development, or coherence; the article states the condition is reversible in principle and that its premise — that authorship ought to be located in the individual — is not culturally universal
target_learners: Emerging adults habitually enlisting generative AI for self-formative dialogue
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing delegated from exercised self-authorship; recognizing un-authored self-narratives
examples: Table 2 distinguishes authorial suspension from the in-between feeling of emerging adulthood, moratorium, diffusion, multiphrenia, and unattained self-authorship, each with candidate operational markers

article_title: When Should Teachers Control AI Generation for Mathematics Visuals?
citation: Zhengxu Li, Junling Wang, and April Yi Wang. (2026). When Should Teachers Control AI Generation for Mathematics Visuals? arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10672
title: In correctness-sensitive educational domains, make correctness auditable: support verifiable, localized correction rather than relying on output quality alone
description: The article argues that in correctness-sensitive domains such as mathematics education, "output quality alone is an insufficient success criterion" and that "Auditability emerges as a foundational design requirement". Teachers evaluated visuals by representational fidelity — whether structure preserved intended mathematical relationships and quantities — and valued post-generation control because it let them inspect, verify, and enforce correctness without inferring hidden system behavior. Systems should make correctness visible and support bounded, local correction that does not cause unintended changes elsewhere.
requirements: Teachers must be able to directly inspect and verify correctness-critical details of generated visuals without needing to infer hidden system behavior.
constraints: The article notes verification in the study relied largely on manual inspection, placing sustained cognitive demands on teachers, and recommends future constraint-aware generation and automatic consistency checks.
target_learners: primary mathematics teachers
target_learning_goals: ensuring instructional visuals faithfully represent quantities, relations, and groupings
examples: In the study, post-gen visuals were editable SVG objects whose local edits were deterministic and immediately visible, letting teachers correct single objects without global side effects.

title: Authored ignorance: felt authorship of an artifact whose genericity its author cannot perceive
description: Authored ignorance is the article's theoretical label for an informational condition in AI-mediated production: a person can feel they directed an artifact while lacking the comparison set needed to judge its position in the output distribution. The article defines it as "felt authorship of an artifact whose genericity its author has no way to perceive, because perceiving it would require the distribution of everyone else's artifacts, which only the platform sees." It builds on the AI ghostwriter effect and psychological ownership theory, and is offered as an interpretation to be tested directly in future work.
requirements: Testing the construct directly requires measuring perceived originality or awareness of genericity, which the article's survey did not include
constraints: The article states the construct is an interpretation to be tested in future work, not a directly measured variable in this study
target_learners: graduate students using generative AI production tools
target_learning_goals: awareness of how generative production tools shape the originality of one's creative output

title: Teoría social cognitiva de la autoeficacia y la agencia humana (Bandura) como marco del andamiaje motivacional
description: La tesis adopta el marco de Bandura: la autoeficacia se define como "las creencias en las propias capacidades para organizar y ejecutar los cursos de acción requeridos para manejar situaciones futuras". En el marco de la teoría social cognitiva se plantean "cuatro características distintivas de la agencia humana: la intención, previsión, auto-reactividad y auto- reflexión". La autoeficacia actúa sobre procesos cognitivos, motivacionales, emocionales y de selección, y es el mecanismo de reflexión más importante; una mayor percepción de autoeficacia mejora el esfuerzo y la recuperación al fracaso, influyendo sobre el logro.

title: Automated counting procedure model of simple addition: the '+' sign pre-activates an abstract procedure, likely scrolling a mental number line, rather than triggering retrieval of stored facts
description: The article advances an alternative to dominant fact-retrieval accounts of simple addition. It proposes that presenting the "+" sign pre-activates an abstract procedure — possibly "a mental representation akin to a mental number line along which individuals' attention could make displacements by one" — which is then executed to solve the problem. Within this model, "automated counting procedures could therefore be limited to additions up to 4 elements", matching the subitizing range, and such procedures "are probably run to completion by experts without awareness", which explains why adults report retrieval. The model predicts sign priming for non-tie additions but not for multiplication, ties, or +0 problems, exactly the pattern observed here in both age groups.
requirements: The priming effect is only observable in individuals with high arithmetic proficiency; the authors note priming effects "cannot be observed, whatever the categories of problems, when we consider the whole population".
constraints: The article states the paradigm's characteristics "do not allow the generalization of our interpretations to the whole population of elderly individuals"; whether less efficient individuals use automated procedures or the paradigm fails to reveal them remains unknown.

citation: Hagger, M. S., & Chatzisarantis, N. L. D. (2016). The Trans-Contextual Model of Autonomous Motivation in Education: Conceptual and Empirical Issues and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315585005
title: Teachers foster autonomous motivation and persistence by providing choice, rationale, and self-directed learning support
description: The article identifies autonomy support as the key means by which social agents foster students' autonomous motivation: "teachers are able to foster higher levels of autonomous motivation and greater behavioral persistence by providing instruction and feedback that focuses on self-directed learning and by giving students choice over, and a rationale for, their actions." Specific autonomy-supportive behaviors include providing choice and meaningful rationale, offering encouragement and positive feedback, avoiding controlling directives, acknowledging students' perspectives, and promoting an exploratory approach toward tasks. This principle grounds Proposition 1 of the trans-contextual model and points to autonomy-supportive programs as an intervention route.
requirements: Teachers must display autonomy-supportive behaviors so that students perceive autonomy support, which correlates with actual teacher support
target_learners: school students in classroom contexts
target_learning_goals: autonomous motivation and self-directed persistence with learning activities
examples: Research mapped specific teacher behaviors supporting autonomy, including providing choice, offering hints, and avoiding controlling commands

article_title: Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning
citation: Daiki Nakamura. (2026). Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6
title: The augmentation–erosion framework: offloading augments learning when the offloaded process is peripheral to the learning goal and erodes it when the process is constitutive
description: The framework treats the educational effect of GenAI as a property of the partition of cognitive labor between learner and machine rather than of the tool. It holds that offloading is augmentative when the handed-off process is peripheral, freeing working-memory resources for germane processing, and erosive when the process is constitutive of the learning target, bypassing the processing learning was supposed to involve. Erosion covers both acquisition erosion (failing to build a competence) and maintenance erosion (decay of an acquired competence through non-exercise). Outcomes are defined relative to a comparison condition, by default unaided work with time on task held constant.
requirements: A specified learning goal against which operations are classified as peripheral or constitutive
A comparison condition (default: unaided work, time on task held constant) against which augmentation and erosion are defined
constraints: A conceptual article advancing propositions as hypotheses to be tested, not data-reported conclusions
Focal outcome is durable, unaided learning assessed at a delay, not AI-assisted performance
target_learners: STEM learners in secondary and undergraduate education
target_learning_goals: Durable, unaided disciplinary competence in STEM practices such as modeling, justification, and proof
examples: Student A offloads data entry, plotting, and parameter fitting but selects and justifies the model herself, an augmentative partition; Student B pastes data and transcribes the AI's answer, an episode at high risk of acquisition erosion

citation: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5
title: Support students' autonomy and agency as they collaboratively work on meaningful and interesting challenges to foster caring about epistemic performance
description: This design principle addresses the fourth aspect of the Apt-AIR framework—caring about and enjoying epistemic performance. The article states that "to foster caring about epistemic performance, our key design principle has been to support students' autonomy and agency as they collaboratively work on meaningful and interesting challenges." The authors observed that "students appeared unlikely to care about aims, ideals, and processes unless they had some agency in choosing and/or applying them."

constraints: The principle was derived from the authors' design observations rather than from controlled experimental comparisons
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students engaged in epistemic inquiry tasks
target_learning_goals: motivation and positive dispositions toward epistemic performance including caring about valuable epistemic aims and ideals
examples: The authors applied this principle in design studies where students collaboratively worked on model-based inquiry and source evaluation challenges

citation: Alexandra Patzak, Xiaorong Zhang. (2025). Blending Teacher Autonomy Support and Provision of Structure in the Classroom for Optimal Motivation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09994-2
title: Autonomy support as a multi-component instructional construct (ten defining components)
description: The review synthesizes how 94 studies conceptualize teacher autonomy support as teachers' efforts to support students' need for autonomy through instructional strategies. A detailed analysis "yielded ten distinct components of autonomy support", the most common being "providing students with choices" and "providing explanatory rationales", plus acknowledging negative feelings, taking students' perspective, promoting students' voice, inviting pursuit of interests, invitational language, need-satisfying activity design, patience, and respect. Definitions of individual components vary across studies, hampering generalizability.
requirements: Studies must define autonomy support via identifiable instructional strategy components for the taxonomy to apply
constraints: Component definitions are inconsistent across studies; e.g., choices are variably described as aligned with interests or merely 'offering choice' without elaboration
target_learners: K-12 and post-secondary students
examples: Offer choice was referenced by 62 studies; provide explanatory rationales by 35; acknowledge negative feelings by 23 (Table 2)

article_title: Stirring a Secret Sauce: A Literature Review on the Conditions and Effects of Authentic Learning
citation: Valentina Nachtigall, David Williamson Shaffer, Nikol Rummel. (2022). Stirring a Secret Sauce: A Literature Review on the Conditions and Effects of Authentic Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1479–1516. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09676-3
title: Synthesized framework of eight design elements of authentic learning settings
description: The review synthesizes four prior operationalizations (Herrington & Oliver 2000; Rule 2006; Betz et al. 2016; Hod & Sagy 2019) into eight main design elements: collaboration, complex problems/tasks, inquiry/investigation, experts/practitioners, real-life/professional setting, real-life materials/cultural tools, authentic assessment, and technology. It states that "authentic learning is assumed to emerge from the interaction of multiple design elements", with rarer elements such as reflection, coaching and scaffolding overlapping with the more common ones.
requirements: Authentic learning settings combine multiple design elements; the review analyzes how the eight elements interact rather than treating any single element as sufficient
constraints: Authentic assessment is treated as a design element rather than an intention of authenticity, and teacher authenticity is excluded because it can hardly be achieved by implementing design elements
target_learners: School students
Undergraduate and vocational learners as represented in the reviewed studies
target_learning_goals: Cognitive outcomes such as knowledge acquisition and problem-solving
Motivational outcomes such as interest and intrinsic motivation
examples: The review's codebook illustrates each element with reviewed studies, e.g., learners visiting an agritourism farm to learn about aquaponics as a real-life/professional setting

citation: Bai, H.; Chan, L.; Luo, A.; Kroesbergen, E.H.; Christie, S. (2026). Creativity in dialogues: How do children interact with parents vs. strangers for generating creative ideas? Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102286
title: Novel coding scheme for cognitive and social-emotional perspective taking in dyadic AUT dialogues
description: A novel observational coding scheme designed by the authors, based on the PAT theory and inspirations from Chiu (2008), applied utterance-by-utterance to videotaped and transcribed AUT sessions. It contains two broad categories, cognitive perspective taking (Listen/understand and Extend/revise) and social-emotional perspective taking (Direct deny/doubt, Polite deny/doubt, Recognize/agree, Appreciate/praise), plus Inviting behavior and Utterance number as controls. Reliability testing showed that "Kappa was 0.63 (95 % CI [0.59,0.66]) for the whole coding scheme (with mutual-exclusive categories)".
requirements: Videotaped, verbatim-transcribed dialogue sessions segmented into utterances, and coders blinded to the study hypotheses applying one mutually exclusive code per utterance.
constraints: Per-category agreement was lower for the disagreement codes: Kappa was 0.40 (95 % CI [0.13, 0.75]) for Direct deny/doubt and 0.50 (95 % CI [0.29, 0.70]) for Polite deny/doubt, described as moderate to substantial inter-coder agreement overall.
target_learners: children aged 4-6 years interacting with adults in creative tasks
target_learning_goals: quantifying social processes (exchange of ideas, open accepting atmosphere) during collaborative creative idea generation
examples: The scheme was applied to 102 dyads' transcripts; five transcripts (incl. 1807 utterances) were double coded to establish inter-coder agreement.

citation: Merkt, M., Lux, S., Hoogerheide, V., van Gog, T., & Schwan, S. (2020). A Change of Scenery: Does the Setting of an Instructional Video Affect Learning? Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000414
title: Competing hypotheses: an authentic video setting as distraction versus as a cue for instructor expertise
description: The article frames two competing theoretical accounts of what an authentic setting does during video learning: the setting may draw the learner's attention away from the content, or it may signal the instructor's expertise and thereby support learning. Experiment 1 was designed to pit these accounts against each other, exploring "whether an authentic setting would serve as a distraction or as a cue for the instructor's expertise." The mixed experimental outcomes across the two experiments left the competition between the hypotheses unresolved.

constraints: The retention benefit observed in Experiment 1 did not replicate in Experiment 2, leaving the hypotheses unresolved.

article_title: How can the blow of math difficulty on elementary school children’s motivational, cognitive, and affective experiences be dampened? The critical role of autonomy-supportive instructions.
citation: Baten, E., Vansteenkiste, M., De Muynck, G., De Poortere, E., Desoete, A. (2020). How Can the Blow of Math Difficulty on Elementary School Children's Motivational, Cognitive and Affective Experiences be Dampened? The Critical Role of Autonomy-Supportive Instructions. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000444
title: Introduce difficult math tasks with autonomy-supportive instructions to buffer their impairing effects
description: When learners must work on tasks that are too difficult for them, the article recommends introducing them in an autonomy-supportive rather than controlling way — using inviting language, offering choice, and providing a meaningful rationale. In the experiment, such instructions "were dampened when the exercises were introduced in an autonomy -supportive manner" in their harmful need-related effects, fully cancelling the autonomy-frustrating effect of difficulty and minimizing its competence-impairing impact. The authors state this is especially valuable for poor performers and children with Mathematical Learning Disabilities.
requirements: The instructional style must include inviting language, choice in how and in what order to solve exercises, and a meaningful rationale, as operationalized in the comic-book vignette.
constraints: The buffering was partial for competence-based experiences: autonomy-supportive instructions minimized but did not cancel out the competence-impairing impact of difficulty.
The style manipulation was vignette-based and one-time; its main effects were limited compared to the difficulty manipulation, and replication with real teachers is needed.
target_learners: Elementary school children learning mathematics, especially poor performers and children with Mathematical Learning Disabilities
target_learning_goals: Maintaining interest, engagement and challenge seeking when working on difficult math exercises
examples: Children read a comic book in which a teacher introduced math exercises either autonomously-supportively (choice, rationale, inviting language) or controllingly (pressure, no rationale, exercises framed as a test) before solving easy-medium or difficult exercises.

title: Authentic learning environment framework for cultivating digital innovation skills

article_title: Autoscoring Anticlimax: A Meta-analytic Understanding of AI's Short-answer Shortcomings and Wording Weaknesses
citation: Michael Hardy. (2026). Autoscoring Anticlimax: A Meta-analytic Understanding of AI's Short-answer Shortcomings and Wording Weaknesses. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04820
title: Autoregressive training objective misalignment account of LLM autoscoring failure
description: The article proposes that LLM short-answer scoring failures follow from the autoregressive pretraining objective, which "rewards fluency, local coherence, and surface-form patterning" rather than the deep semantic comprehension, inferential reasoning, and rubric-grounded ordinal decision rules that scoring child-written text demands. Decoder-only architectures optimize unidirectional likelihood p(xt|x<t), while the signal that matters in grading is often bidirectional and non-local, better supported by encoder objectives that denoise and model p(xmasked|x context). This account explains the meta-analytic regularities: meaning dependence penalties, decoder underperformance, tokenizer/vocabulary effects, and prompt sensitivity.
requirements: Models trained autoregressively on internet text; scoring tasks requiring rubric-consistent ordinal judgments of child-written responses
constraints: The article states vocabulary size and tokenizer family are partially confounded with model families, so causal interpretations should be made cautiously; only the direction (and not the magnitude) of estimated coefficients should be considered
target_learners: K-12 students whose written short answers are scored
target_learning_goals: Trustworthy automated assessment of student learning from short constructed responses
examples: The meta-regression of 890 QWK results shows the read indicator negative across specifications and the gpt coefficient negative in the Bayesian fit, which the article links to autoregressive bias

article_title: Does Repeated Reading Improve Reading Fluency and Comprehension for Struggling Adolescent Readers?
citation: Still, K. L., & Flynt, C. A. (2012). Does Repeated Reading Improve Reading Fluency and Comprehension for Struggling Adolescent Readers? JAASEP, Winter 2012. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Does+Repeated+Reading+Improve+Reading+Fluency+and+Comprehension+for+Struggling+Adolescent+Readers
title: Automaticity theory: non-automatic decoding consumes finite cognitive energy needed for comprehension
description: Automaticity theory, originating with LaBerge and Samuels in 1974, explains why fluent decoding matters for comprehension: readers who have not achieved automaticity in word recognition must spend finite cognitive energy on decoding, energy that is taken from comprehending the text. The article uses this theory to motivate the repeated reading intervention, since repetition is said to allow "the deepening of traces and the freeing up of attention" so readers can focus on comprehension. It underpins the study's expectation that fluency practice should support comprehension.
requirements: Readers must first achieve automaticity in word recognition, built on phonemic awareness, phonics word-attack strategies, and strong orthographic representations, before cognitive energy is freed for comprehension
target_learners: struggling adolescent readers with learning disabilities
examples: The study's repeated peer reading treatment was designed so daily rereading of the same passage would build automaticity and thereby free attention for comprehension.

citation: Negari, G. M., Azizi, A., & Arani, D. K. (2018). Investigating the Effectiveness of Audio Input Enhancement on EFL Learners’ Retention of Intensifiers. International Journal of Instruction, 11(1), 123-138. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1119a
title: Use audio input enhancement to draw EFL learners' attention to target grammatical structures, but pair it with deeper processing for long-term retention
description: The article recommends audio input enhancement as a classroom technique for grammar teaching in EFL contexts with limited L2 input exposure: "Audio input enhancement can be applied as a technique to draw learners' attention to special grammatical structures of input and, consequently, facilitates their acquisition of the targeted forms." However, because the delayed-test gain was not significant and enhancement was said to produce shallow processing, learners must attend to acquired forms more consciously to retain them long-term, and material designers should develop new materials raising audio input in writing-dominant classes.
requirements: Additional processing on input beyond the enhancement itself is required for long-term retention, per the article's discussion citing Reinder (2005)

target_learning_goals: Acquisition and long-term retention of instructed grammatical structures
examples: In the study, the experimental group's teacher increased the volume of listening files containing intensifiers and provided short explanations at learners' request, while the control group received only printed files

article_title: Short-Term and Long-Term Retention of Vocabulary through Authentic Subtitled Videos
citation: Nader Asadi Aidinlou & Alireza Moradinejad. (2016). Short-term and Long-term Retention of Vocabulary through Authentic Subtitled Videos. Advances in Language and Literary Studies. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.5p.14
title: Taxonomies of authenticity in language teaching materials
description: The article reviews competing taxonomies of authenticity as an organizing framework for materials design. Breen identified four types, including "Authenticity of the texts which we may use as input data for our students" and authenticity of learners' interpretations, tasks, and classroom social situation. Taylor identified three types — language, task, and situation — arguing they are not clearly distinguished. The study itself targets authenticity of use (task) rather than of language.
requirements: The article states the study focused on authenticity of the way materials were used rather than authenticity of the materials themselves, since both groups used authentic materials
constraints: Taylor's three types are argued by the article to be not clearly distinguished
target_learners: EFL learners at advanced level
examples: The study manipulated authenticity of use: the experimental group watched subtitled sitcoms while the control group received traditional instruction on vocabulary drawn from the same subtitles

article_title: Effects of Audiovisual Media on L2 Listening Comprehension: A Preliminary Study in French
citation: Shannon R. Becker and Jessica L. Sturm. (2017). Effects of Audiovisual Media on L2 Listening Comprehension: A Preliminary Study in French. CALICO Journal. https://doi.org/10.1558/cj.26754
title: Four-week daily audiovisual-media listening treatment embedded in second-semester French instruction
description: The treatment consisted of daily listening activities using online audiovisual media excerpts, taking approximately 10 minutes each across 13 class periods, embedded in the regular course so that instructional time and content were equivalent to the control group and "the only difference was task type." Activities used pre- and postlistening tasks to process aural input from the excerpts, and the same instructor taught both sections to keep teaching style consistent. Students were unaware of the difference in instruction.
requirements: Equivalent instructional time and content across conditions
Same instructor across groups to remove teaching differences as a confound
Pre- and postlistening activities surrounding the audiovisual excerpts
constraints: The article notes the short four-week time frame limited learners' contact with the experimental instruction
target_learners: postsecondary second-semester French students
native English-speaking L2 learners of French
examples: In one lesson, both groups discussed vocabulary from a photograph of people in disarrayed clothing; the experimental group then watched two short online laundry-tips clips with brainstorming and comprehension questions while the control group completed an oral sentence-completion task and paired discussion

article_title: The Effect of Using Video Technology on Improving Reading Comprehension of Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners
citation: Amir Mohammadian, Amin Saed, Younes Shahi. (2018). The Effect of Using Video Technology on Improving Reading Comprehension of Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.9n.2p.17
title: Use authentic video materials as part of an active learning strategy when teaching EFL reading comprehension
description: The article argues that video materials expose learners to language as used by native speakers in real contexts rather than lesson-designed language, and that because "watching video is a passive activity, it needs to be used as part of an active learning strategy in order to be an effective tool". Videos combine visual and aural information, which the authors link to dual coding enhancing encoding.
requirements: Videos must be embedded in an active learning strategy rather than used as passive viewing, per the article's quoted caution.
constraints: The supporting experiment involved only male, intermediate-level, Persian-speaking high-school students aged 16-18 in Chabahar, Iran.
target_learners: intermediate EFL learners in secondary school
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension in English as a foreign language
examples: In the study, the experimental group used educational video files for 15 weeks (three sessions per week) while the control group received regular instruction with little communicative practice of reading skills.

article_title: The Effect of Using Authentic Task on Teaching Adjectives
citation: Shadi Rastegaran. (2016). The Effect of Using Authentic Task on Teaching Adjectives. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 7(2), 18-24. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.2p.18
title: Teach adjectives through authentic tasks rather than traditional vocabulary lists, because authentic tasks rely on learners' experiences and reality
description: This principle holds that vocabulary, including adjectives, is best taught through authentic tasks that "relies on learners’ experiences and reality to facilitate learning", rather than through word lists for memorization. The article's experiment supported it: learners taught adjectives via authentic zodiac-sign texts significantly outperformed those given dictionary extracts. The author concludes that teachers and material developers should provide authentic materials as encouraging and leading to better learning.
requirements: Authentic tasks must be purposeful and engaging and model how people solve real problems, as the article defines authentic tasks
constraints: Evidence is from one quasi-experimental study with intact groups of Iranian intermediate EFL learners learning adjectives only
target_learners: Iranian intermediate EFL learners
target_learning_goals: Adjective and vocabulary learning in a second language
examples: Group E read 12 short texts about the 12 zodiac signs, looked up unknown words in dictionaries, and each session wrote a short description of a classmate or family member born under the same sign using the learned adjectives

title: Autotutor intelligent tutoring system for speaking practice with speech recognition and pronunciation diagrams
description: The Autotutor software is the computer-assisted intelligent tutoring system used as the treatment platform. It supports natural speech tutoring via "a five-step conversation frame", acts as teacher and student, and lets learners speak instead of movie characters after watching a video file. After recording the student's voice it "drew diagram of the speaker's pronunciation", and students can at any time refer to the autotutor and ask for help.

constraints: The article identifies the system's main weakness as its incapability to hold learner-learner and learner-teacher conversations during the learning process

target_learning_goals: Improving English speaking ability (fluency and coherence, pronunciation, lexical resource, grammatical range and accuracy)
examples: Groups A and B practiced speaking with autotutor across ten treatment sessions within a 13-session semester-long study; group A requested autotutor's help and hints, group B self-corrected with minimal hint use

article_title: Instructional Effects of Syntactic Parsing on Chinese College Students' EFL Reading Rates
citation: Xiaokan Chen, Hongmei Li, Min Gui. (2018). Instructional Effects of Syntactic Parsing on Chinese College Students’ EFL Reading Rates. Journal of Education and Training Studies, Vol. 6, No. 11. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v6i11.3470
title: Automaticity Theory and Attentional Resource Emancipation as the framework explaining why lower-level parsing automaticity frees resources for comprehension
description: The article draws on an information-processing account in which reading comprises lower-level processes (word recognition, syntactic parsing, semantic proposition formation) and higher-level processes (text model, situation model, background knowledge, executive control). Because cognitive resources are limited, "the lower-level processes need to be automatized" so resources can be reserved for demanding higher-level processing. The authors state their results are "consistent with two theories: Automaticity Theory and Attentional Resource Emancipation". Syntactic parsing is defined as processing words "in larger units of structure" to extract grammatical information for clause-level meaning construction.
requirements: Learners must develop fast and automatic syntactic parsing through sufficient training, since overt grammatical knowledge alone does not yield automatic parsing
Instruction must be embedded with practice so parsing becomes effortless rather than deliberate
constraints: The authors note a dearth of clear empirical evidence for automaticity effects despite strong theoretical establishment
The framework was tested here only with Chinese college freshmen reading English, with a medium effect size
target_learners: Chinese college EFL students
L2 readers of English
examples: The experimental group received 12 weekly 15-minute sessions of syntactic parsing lectures and in-class and homework parsing practice embedded in the normal curriculum

article_title: Learning Authentic Leadership in New Zealand: A Learner-Centred Methodology and Evaluation
citation: Maree Roche. (2010). Learning Authentic Leadership In New Zealand: A Learner-Centred Methodology And Evaluation. American Journal of Business Education, Volume 3, Number 3. https://clutejournals.com/index.php/AJBE
title: Authenticity as a developmental, relational process of multiple selves rather than a fixed true self
description: Drawing on Kernis (2003), Harter (2002), Erickson (1995) and Luthans, Youssef and Avolio (2006), the article presents authenticity as self-referential, non-dualistic, non-linear and dialectic, achieved in levels rather than as an either/or condition. People possess multiple actual and possible selves; through self-awareness and self-development strategies the possible self is gradually actualized into the true self, so "authenticity development is a personal and dynamic process". The authentic self is also developed through interactions with others, giving it a relational, socially constructed aspect.
requirements: Self-awareness and self-development strategies to understand strengths and limitations of actual and potential selves
Environments that support free self-expression, since controlled situations lacking free expression are likely to impede the authentic self
constraints: The article notes a pitfall would be to assume there is a non-changing and singular self
target_learners: developing leaders and leadership students
target_learning_goals: recognizing the role of others in developing authenticity
examples: The article reports Harter (2002) used the self-awareness, possible and actual self process in counseling adolescents with promising results

citation: Sushanta Kumar Roul. (2014). Language Development of the Preschool Children: The Effects of an Audio-Visual Intervention Program in Delhi. International Journal of Instruction, 7(1). https://www.e-iji.net
title: Audio-Visual Intervention Program for preschool language development
description: A magazine-format audio-visual program used as the experimental treatment in the Delhi study, delivered through the preschool teacher after a two-day orientation covering the importance of audio-visual aids, selected audio programs, and demonstration via simulation and micro-teaching. Each program is "in a magazine format and of 15 minutes duration" and "includes conversation, song, story, drama, riddles, music and sound effects and fun and humor in it". Its effectiveness was tested against a matched control group on listening comprehension and vocabulary.
requirements: A preschool teacher trained in a two-day orientation on using audio-visual aids and conducting the sessions
constraints: Evaluated in one preschool in Rohini, Delhi with 100 L.K.G. children; effectiveness beyond this setting was not tested
target_learners: preschool children (L.K.G., ages 2–5)
examples: The program was delivered to the experimental group while a matched control group received no treatment, with pre-testing used to ensure group homogeneity

citation: Melike Özüdoğru, Fatma Özüdoğru. (2017). The Effect of Situated Learning on Students' Vocational English Learning. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(11): 2037-2044. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.051120

description: Based on their results, the authors recommend that instructors use varied authentic materials and peer collaboration in vocational English courses. They suggest instructors "should use a wide range of materials in class" and have students read accounting-related books and magazines, write e-mails, and watch advertisements and films in English to make connections between classroom English and the real world, and that "cooperative learning based on the principles and practices of situated learning can be employed by instructors in class".

group structures that allow students to share ideas and learn from each other
constraints: the recommendation rests on a four-week study with a small sample that the authors say restricts generalization

target_learning_goals: vocational English vocabulary and communication skills
examples: In the study, students practiced English by writing e-mails, preparing videos with their peers, working on a balance sheet and sales report
