article_title: What Is Needed for Correct Pronunciation: A Model or a Concern?
citation: Kayaoglu, M. N. & Caylak, N. (2013). What is needed for correct pronunciation: a model or a concern? Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 53, 269-290. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1075217
title: Audio Articulation Method (AAM) model lesson structure
description: The Audio Articulation Method, proposed by Demirezen (2004), is a pronunciation teaching model "designed to fill this gap in the field of pronunciation teaching" by rehabilitating fossilized segmental errors within a single class hour. Its basic steps involve the teacher identifying the problematic core sound, preparing a corpus of 50-100 words including that sound and its nearest pair, singling out minimal pairs, developing tongue twisters and idiomatic chunks, and stimulating further awareness through experiential practices.

Corpus of 50-100 words including the problem sound and its nearest pair
Minimal pairs extracted for practice
Tongue twisters, proverbs, idioms, mottoes, or cliche expressions developed in chunks
constraints: Designed for students studying English Language Teaching at university level
No reliable diagnostic tool for determining whether errors are fossilized
Fossilization issue excluded from the scope of this study

Turkish EFL learners with segmental pronunciation difficulties
target_learning_goals: Rehabilitation of fossilized segmental pronunciation errors
examples: Model lesson one is devoted to one or two specific sounds, approximately 45-50 minutes per class

article_title: Effects of Autonomy Supportive vs. Controlling Teachers' Behavior on Students' Achievements
citation: Hofferber, N., Eckes, A., & Wilde, M. (2014). Effects of Autonomy Supportive vs. Controlling Teachers' Behavior on Students' Achievements. European Journal of Educational Research, 3(4), 177-184. http://www.eurojedu.com
title: Use autonomy supportive teacher behaviors to facilitate deep and effective student learning
description: The article concludes that autonomy supportive teacher behaviors can be recommended to facilitate deep and effective student learning, particularly for conceptual knowledge acquisition. Teachers should offer choices, provide informative feedback, use non-controlling language (e.g., 'You could...'), and avoid controlling procedures such as marks or red-pen corrections. This recommendation is grounded in the study's finding that autonomy support significantly improved conceptual learning while rote learning remained unaffected.
requirements: Teachers must genuinely offer students choices (e.g., group membership, task order, time allocation) rather than prescribing solutions
Feedback should be informative rather than controlling, and teachers should avoid controlling language such as 'You must' or 'You should'
constraints: The evidence comes from a single three-hour biology unit with seventh graders; the authors note controlling behavior did not negatively affect rote learning, so the advantage applies specifically to higher cognitive level learning
target_learners: seventh grade middle school students (Realschule)
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge acquisition and application of knowledge to modified contexts
examples: In the A-treatment, the teacher gave informative feedback ('You observed the climbing properties of the mouse well'), allowed students to choose group members and task order, corrected with a green pen, gave no marks, and used expressions like 'You could (…)'

In the C-treatment, the teacher gave controlling feedback ('You did the work just as I wanted you to do it'), chose group members and task order, corrected with a red pen, gave marks, and used expressions like 'You must (...)'

title: Use audio-only rather than video modality when assessing L2 listening comprehension with lecture texts
description: The study suggests audio-only delivery may be more favorable than video for listening assessment, as visual elements can distract test takers. The authors found "the audio delivery was more favorable" and recommend considering modality effects when designing listening tests. This principle applies when using lecture-style texts where visuals may impose a cognitive load.
requirements: Test content should be lecture-style audio or video recordings with equivalent content across modalities
constraints: Findings are not conclusive; motivation, topic familiarity, note-taking habits, and pausing may affect outcomes
target_learners: First-grade ELT university students with B1-B2 proficiency
examples: The study administered four lecture texts (iceberg analogy, American culture, semiotics, language learning) in audio-only or video-only format to two randomly assigned groups

Faculty review and tiering of prescriptions by difficulty

citation: Zhang Simin, Li Jiao, Deng Cui, Zheng Sheng. (2026). CBL combined with MDT mode in clinical teaching of liver cancer: a randomized controlled study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09212-9

description: The theoretical framework underlying CBL-MDT integration draws upon constructivist learning theory and social cognitive theory. Expert models who explicitly articulate reasoning processes
constraints: Resource-intensive nature of MDT teaching requires institutional support
Transition from passive learning to active participation may initially discomfort some students

examples: The teaching team curated five representative HCC cases spanning the disease spectrum, and specialists from six disciplines participated in structured MDT discussions following authentic clinical conference protocols.

description: The article recommends that autonomous learning behaviors—consistent attendance, in-class engagement, and postclass review—"may be encouraged through simple, feasible course designs such as clear expectation setting, periodic interactive prompts, and structured review opportunities". article_title: Medical Students' Perception of Automated Note Feedback After Simulated Encounters.
citation: S. Bansal, M. Yadav, J. Zhou, R. A. Ebert‐Allen, R. M. Klute, W. F. Bond, S. Bhat. (2025). Medical Students' Perception of Automated Note Feedback After Simulated Encounters. The Clinical Teacher 22(6): e70273. https://doi.org/10.1111/tct.70273
title: Use automated NLP-based feedback as a complement to faculty feedback rather than a replacement
description: The article supports using automated NLP-based patient note feedback alongside faculty feedback. Students stated the automated process "could be an addition to that process" rather than replacing personalized preceptor feedback. The two methods offer complementary strengths: automated feedback provides clarity and ease of comparison while faculty feedback provides trust and contextual reasoning.

Occasional errors in phrase recognition and false positives

description: The study's measurement instruments consist of a 9-item demographic form, a researcher-developed 15-item true/false cardiac auscultation knowledge test scored 0 to 15, and an 18-item skill checklist scored on a 3-point scale (0 = Not done; 1 = partially done; 2 = completely done) with a maximum of 36. description: Because the blended training improved theoretical performance, self-directed learning and critical thinking but not clinical operation skills, the article recommends strengthening hands-on practice. As the authors put it, "The lack of impact of “Learning, Thinking & Conveying” training on clinical operations skills may indicate the need to augment the practical, hands-on component of the nursing course to extend the benefits to clinical proficiency." constraints: In this study practical training was similar for both groups to ensure quality control, which may explain the null skills result

title: E-library of authentic patient video vignettes for mental status examination training
description: An e-library of 23 video vignettes of brief authentic patient interviews (edited to 8–12 min) with adjoining MSEs written by three faculty psychiatrists, hosted on a secure educational platform (Kaltura). Students follow an instructional sequence: "read a brief note about the patient, watch the video, write their own MSE, and compare it with the provided expert MSE summary." Access was restricted by confidentiality rules and granted per clinical attachment. Diagnoses were omitted to maintain focus on the descriptive task.

constraints: Videos were edited to 8–12 min as recommended; brief exposure of about 3 weeks may have been insufficient to fully develop MSE skills

examples: In the trial, the Full group's mean satisfaction with how much the authentic videos helped learn MSE was 4.4 (SD 0.7) on a 1–5 Likert scale, and students reported watching a mean of 7.3 videos (SD 5.2)

article_title: Enhancing laparoscopic surgery training: a comparative study of traditional models and automated error detection system.
citation: Luo Yitian, Wang Jingjie, Yan Zongting, He Jingjing, Fu Liye, Wang Shenghan, Han Ying, Fu Yaoyu, Wang Xiandi, Li Kang, Yin Rong, Pu Dan. (2025). Enhancing laparoscopic surgery training: a comparative study of traditional models and automated error detection system. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07242-3
title: Integrate automated objective error-detection feedback into surgical simulation training to reduce errors and mitigate overconfidence
description: The article advocates pairing simulation practice with automated, objective, real-time error feedback so trainees can locate and correct mistakes during the task rather than relying on subjective instructor evaluation or self-assessment. The findings "advocate for adopting AEDS in surgical education to standardize training outcomes, mitigate overconfidence, and improve patient safety", because subjective self-assessment alone left novices systematically unaware of their errors. The principle extends the general feedback mechanism of the AEDS beyond its specific hardware.
requirements: A sensing mechanism that objectively records operational errors in real time
A feedback display trainees can consult during practice to adjust their operating mode
constraints: Findings reflect early skill acquisition in inexperienced undergraduates and may not transfer to residents or advanced procedural modules
Only contact-type errors are captured; broader error types require additional sensing such as force measurement
target_learners: novice surgical trainees and medical students learning procedural skills
target_learning_goals: technical precision in minimally invasive procedures
examples: 40 novices were randomized to AEDS-enhanced versus traditional training with total practice time standardized at 20 minutes
The AEDS screen displayed cumulative operational errors and total operation duration during practice

citation: Van Kelsey, Tasawar Sana, Brendel Elaina B. K., Law Camille, Mahajan Anisha, Brownell‐Riddell Carissa, Diamond Natalia, Ritchie Kerry, Monk Jennifer M. (2025). Using a 'Students as Partners' model to develop an authentic assessment promoting employability skills in undergraduate life science education. FEBS Open Bio 15(3): 506–522. https://doi.org/10.1002/2211-5463.13941
title: Three principles of authentic assessment: realism, cognitive challenge, and evaluative judgment
description: The article defines authentic assessment (AA) as assessment that replicates professional workplace expectations and is organized around three principles. As printed: "There are three principles of an AA: (a) realism (linking course knowledge to everyday life), (b) cognitive challenge (higher order thinking and problem‐solving), and (c) evaluative judgment (performance self‐evaluation using clear criteria and receiving feedback)". The article uses this framework both to design the Data Extraction Assignment and to interpret student outcomes, arguing AA can develop employability skills such as scientific literacy and communication.
requirements: Clear criteria and feedback opportunities so students can exercise evaluative judgment
constraints: The article notes providing written feedback with revision and regrading is a challenge with limited instructor resources or in large class sizes
target_learners: undergraduate STEM/life science students
target_learning_goals: employability skill development including scientific literacy, communication, critical thinking and evaluative judgment
examples: The Data Extraction Assignment operationalized the principles: realistic workplace communication outputs, higher-order integration of primary literature, and a rubric-based self-assessment component

article_title: Reciprocal Relationships Between Parental Involvement and Academic Performance in Early Adolescence: A Two-Year Longitudinal Study in China.
citation: Yi Yang. (2025). Reciprocal Relationships Between Parental Involvement and Academic Performance in Early Adolescence: A Two-Year Longitudinal Study in China. Journal of Youth and Adolescence, 54(4), 876–889. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10964-024-02102-7
title: Advise parents of Chinese early adolescents to adopt child-centered, autonomy-supportive involvement rather than behavioral control
description: The article recommends that, given the varied impacts of different involvement forms, "Chinese parents are advised to adopt more child-centered and autonomy-supportive forms of parental involvement in their children's learning". It specifies concrete practices: daily communication about school life, educational trips, and close connection with teachers. It also cautions that responsibility should not fall on parents alone, since communities and schools shape opportunities for involvement.
requirements: Parents need access to communication channels with teachers and schools kept open and available for all

target_learning_goals: Academic performance in Chinese, English, and Mathematics
examples: The cross-lagged analysis found education discussion (β = 0.13) positively predicted later performance while behavioral control (β = −0.05) negatively predicted it, grounding the recommendation

article_title: Assessment IS learning: developing a student-centred approach for assessment in Higher Education.
citation: Rutherford S, Pritchard C, Francis N. (2024). Assessment IS learning: developing a student‐centred approach for assessment in Higher Education. FEBS Open Bio. https://doi.org/10.1002/2211-5463.13921
title: Align assessments with discipline-specific, real-world skills to make them meaningful and authentic
description: Assessments gain meaning for students when they mimic or parallel the actual performative skills needed in working life—often termed authentic assessment. The review reports that 'assessments aligned to discipline‐specific skills and activities create meaningful learning environments for the student, reduce cognitive load and foster greater engagement and ownership of the activity'. Students who engage meaningfully are more likely to internalise content, apply it externally, apply substantial effort, and be far less likely to want to cheat or take shortcuts. Making assessments authentic enhances assessment 'as' learning, developing graduate competencies through authoring or performing the assessment.
requirements: Meaningful assessment should connect personally with students' own interests, goals, ambitions, expectations or experiences
constraints: Traditional modalities such as multiple-choice tests, essays and invigilated examinations still perform useful functions of testing knowledge, critical analysis and minimising misconduct potential
target_learners: higher education bioscience students
target_learning_goals: developing graduate competencies and disciplinary skills through assessment
examples: The article lists authentic bioscience examples: writing a scientific paper or report, developing a grant proposal outline, a short scientific presentation, reframing essays as position papers for a biotech company, and framing multiple-choice tests as problem-solving or data evaluation; contextualising knowledge aids retention
key_sources: Rutherford S, Pritchard C, Francis N. (2024). Assessment IS learning: developing a student‐centred approach for assessment in Higher Education. FEBS Open Bio. https://doi.org/10.1002/2211-5463.13921
